decision.explanation: Factor: f(x)=(x+3)(x-1)/[(2x+1)(x-1)]. Canceling x-1 leaves (x+3)/(2x+1), with a hole at x=1. The remaining denominator vanishes at x=-1/2, the only vertical asymptote.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
We start by factoring the function as much as possible and canceling the common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+2x-3}{2{x}^{2}-x-1} & =\frac{(x-1)(x+3)}{(2x+1)(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+3)}{(2x+1)\cancel{(x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{x+3}{2x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
2x+1=0\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So the *only* vertical asymptote is at $x=-\frac{1}{2}.$

after.worked_solution:
First, let's put the two terms over a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+3}-\frac{1}{x-6} & =\frac{x-6-(x+3)}{(x+3)(x-6)}=-\frac{9}{(x+3)(x-6)}\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we proceed to set the denominator equal to zero and get

$$
(x+3)(x-6)=0\,⟹\,x=-3\,,\,x=6.
$$

Therefore, the vertical asymptotes are at $x=-3$ and $x=6.$

We start by factoring the function as much as possible and canceling the common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4x-12}{3{x}^{2}-9x} & =\frac{4(x-3)}{3x(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{4\cancel{(x-3)}}{3x\cancel{(x-3)}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3x}\end{aligned}

$$
